summary:
Buryatia, an autonomous republic of the Russian Federation, stands under the national framework applied across every Russian region. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) records no region-specific findings: it sets out the conditions in force throughout the country, and those conditions govern what a transgender visitor to Buryatia can expect to face.

Legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care were banned outright in 2023, when the law prohibiting gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes on official documents took effect; the Home Office notes that trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in the same year. Same-sex activity is not criminalised, but same-sex marriage and gender transition are prohibited. No discrimination legislation based on sexual orientation or gender identity covers housing, healthcare or employment anywhere in the country.

The expanded "propaganda" statute criminalises public expression that "justifies" gender transition. Offences carry fines of up to 400,000 roubles (about £3,600) for individuals or up to 15 days' detention, and a repeat offence can bring criminal prosecution with up to four years in prison. Foreigners who breach these provisions face arrest, up to 15 days' detention and deportation, and official national government warnings tell LGBT travellers of this directly.

In November 2023 the Supreme Court designated the "international LGBT movement" an extremist organisation, with the ruling entering into force in January 2024. Participation in that movement is punishable by two to six years' imprisonment and organising it by six to ten years. Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions tied to the designation as of 30 June 2025: approximately 98 administrative and three criminal.

Enforcement has been sustained rather than sporadic. Between December 2022 and March 2024 at least 139 people were affected by enforcement of anti-LGBT+ laws. Between January 2024 and June 2025 at least 20 people faced criminal charges under the designation, of whom two were sentenced to prison and one died by suicide in pretrial detention; a further 81 people across 98 court cases were found guilty of administrative offences for displaying banned symbols, with fines up to 2,000 roubles and repeat displays punishable under the criminal code by up to four years. On 15 May 2025 investigators charged three publishing-house staff under article 282.2 for selling fiction exploring LGBT themes, an offence carrying up to 12 years.

The Home Office assesses that trans people, publicly active LGBT+ advocates and those in the North Caucasus are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution, and affirms that LGBT+ people constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention — the standard applied to UK asylum claims. The US State Department advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, and carries warnings directed at LGBT travellers; a foreign-government travel advisory also states that official support is "very limited" in parts of the country.
tangentialFactors:
The post-designation crackdown moved fast. On 17 January 2024, within 48 hours of the Supreme Court's ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly bars in Moscow, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, while at least two other venues were raided the same night.

Arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ+ life through 2025, according to The Moscow Times (23 June 2025), which reported a queer woman in St Petersburg describing herself as "a second-class citizen" after the extremist designation. In December 2024 the Associated Press reported that a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.

Physical coercion against transgender people is separately documented. BBC Russian (27 July 2024) followed "Ada", a transgender woman lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping when police responded to a phone she had found. The case is from Siberia rather than Buryatia, but it illustrates the coercion trans people may face from within their own families, including through institutional detention.

Volume as well as severity is rising. Meduza reported on 19 June 2025 that cases under the propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade and that fines under those statutes brought more than 60 million roubles ($765,300) into the state budget in the two years preceding. Human Rights Watch has called on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing Russia.
localsOnly:
Residents of Buryatia live under the same statute set as visitors, but with no exit and no defence in domestic law: there is no anti-discrimination legislation covering housing, healthcare or employment on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, and legal gender recognition is unavailable, so residents cannot amend the sex marker on official documents at all.

Participation in the designated "international LGBT movement" carries two to six years' imprisonment and organising it six to ten years, while propaganda offences bring fines up to 400,000 roubles or 15 days' detention and up to four years on a repeat. Displaying banned symbols is an administrative offence drawing fines up to 2,000 roubles, escalating to the criminal code and up to four years after a repeat.

At least 139 people were affected by enforcement of anti-LGBT+ laws between December 2022 and March 2024, and 101 extremism-related convictions had been issued by 30 June 2025. The Home Office assessment that trans people constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention is the standard against which a resident leaving the country would be assessed for UK asylum.

The UK Home Office note records no region-specific findings for Buryatia: the conditions it documents are national, and no separate regional finding qualifies, moderates or worsens them for this republic.
outOfScopeNotes:
No enforcement data specific to Buryatia was found in the source inventory. Whether Buryatia's own authorities have conducted bar raids, issued propaganda fines, or brought extremism charges is not sourced, and the national totals cited here are not disaggregated by region.

Local support infrastructure — legal aid, trans-specific healthcare provision, or LGBT organisations operating openly in Buryatia — is not covered by any source in the inventory and remains unresolved. The availability of any avenue for changing documents within the republic is likewise not sourced beyond the national ban.

The conversion-therapy detention documented by BBC Russian took place near Novosibirsk, not in Buryatia; it is reported here as evidence of the coercion trans people face nationally and is not attributed to this region.

The eighteenfold growth in propaganda cases and the 60-million-rouble fine total rest on a single news outlet's reporting and have not been independently corroborated in these sources. The cause and circumstances of the December 2024 pretrial death reported by the Associated Press are also unresolved in the inventory.
